reasons: This is a research and planning document, not software, so there is nothing to run or test in the usual sense.
Part 16 lists facts not yet verified and decisions still open, including the trademark search and counsel review.
Some long lines were cut in the copy used for this review, so not every detail was checked.

terms.meaning: The markup language that gives a web page its structure, such as headings, tables and links.
The styling language that sets colours, fonts, spacing and layout on a web page.
A named value, such as a colour, stored once and reused in many places.
A styling rule that applies only in certain conditions, such as dark mode or a narrow phone screen.
A link that jumps to a named place further down the same page.
A drawing format made of shapes that stays sharp at any size.
Model Context Protocol, a standard way for AI assistants to call outside tools and data sources.
A widely used database that stores records in organised tables.
A fast store for short-lived data, often used to share live updates.
Two ways for a server to push live updates to a browser without the browser asking again and again.
The slow first start of a server that has been idle, when its memory is empty.
A score that rises or falls after each result, depending on how surprising the result was.

depends_on: External ALTER EGO landing concept page on claude.ai

sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Page setup and colour rules
sections.what: Sets up the page metadata, loads the Archivo font and defines the colour palette. The palette is stored once as named values and switches automatically to a dark version when the reader's device is set to dark mode. It also sets basic spacing, link style and the focus outline used by keyboard users.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the look consistent across the whole page and lets it follow the reader's light or dark setting.
sections.watch_out: The colours are written in three places (default, system dark mode and forced dark mode), so a colour change must be made in all three.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Layout, headings and tables
sections.what: Sets the page width, the title block, the contents layout, heading styles, tables, callout boxes and the step flow boxes. On narrow screens the contents list moves above the text and the flow boxes stack on top of each other.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps a long report readable on both phones and desktop screens.
sections.watch_out: Tables have a minimum width, so on small phones they scroll sideways instead of squashing their columns.

sections.name: File setup (part 3)
sections.title: Icons, sources list and motion
sections.what: Defines a hidden set of sport pictogram drawings that the page reuses by name, the row that shows them, the journey boxes and the sources list. It also turns off animations for readers whose devices ask for reduced motion.
sections.why: Likely reason: storing each icon once keeps the page light, and the motion setting supports readers sensitive to movement.
sections.watch_out: The icon drawings are long single lines, so editing one means finding its name among many similar lines.

sections.name: File setup (part 4)
sections.title: Header, contents and summary
sections.what: Builds the top bar with the ALTER EGO name and a link to the landing concept, the title block and the contents list. It then opens part 1, the summary, which argues the core idea and lists the decisions locked so far, such as the public persona names and the rule that there is no real money.
sections.why: Likely reason: a summary at the top lets a reader grasp the whole plan quickly, and the contents list helps them jump to any part.
sections.watch_out: The contents links and citation numbers are typed by hand, so renaming or renumbering a part can silently break a link.

sections.name: File setup (part 5)
sections.title: Codebase review and fix list
sections.what: Part 2 reviews the existing Hitman app. It uses a table of findings graded critical, high, medium or gap, showing where each problem lives and how to fix it. Part 3 turns those fixes into nine ordered steps, each with a done-when test. The section ends by starting part 4 on how AI agents are now built.
sections.why: Likely reason: the owner needs to know what to repair before building anything new, so the fixes come first.
sections.watch_out: This is a snapshot of an older version of the app. Confirm each finding against the current code before acting on it.

sections.name: File setup (part 6)
sections.title: Target architecture and early market notes
sections.what: Describes the intended design in layers: data sources, adapters, an event store, plain-code models, AI agents, guard checks and the user-facing surfaces. It sets a common data model, which assigns AI model tiers to different jobs, and a build-process plan. It then opens the market section with fan habits and money flows, and ends with a callout on India's online gaming law.
sections.why: Likely reason: the model is meant to keep AI output checkable, since the text says models should only reason over numbers the lower layers have computed and can trace.
sections.watch_out: The gaming law callout is the authors' reading of the law, not legal advice. Counsel should confirm it before any money-related feature is considered.

sections.name: File setup (part 7)
sections.title: Big tech moves and funded startups
sections.what: Two tables. The first lists what big tech companies and sports leagues have launched, with a note on what each means for ALTER EGO. The second lists funded sports companies, the amounts they raised and the lesson the authors drew from each.
sections.why: Likely reason: it shows where the market is crowded and where the product can stand apart.
sections.watch_out: Funding amounts and dates come from news reports and are shown as those reports state them, so they may be wrong or out of date.

sections.name: File setup (part 8)
sections.title: Open data, research and white space
sections.what: Three tables. The first lists open and licensed data sources by sport, with what each gives and its limits. The second lists research papers and what the product can learn from them. The third maps product spaces, showing which are crowded, which are open and what the team's stance is on each.
sections.why: Likely reason: the data table tells the team what it can build on, and the white space table explains why the product is shaped the way it is.
sections.watch_out: The Machina sports-skills data is marked personal, non-commercial use only, which would conflict with a commercial product unless a licence is obtained.

sections.name: File setup (part 9)
sections.title: Product story, pillars and fan journeys
sections.what: Explains what ALTER EGO is for fans: the positioning, the origin of the nickname story, four main pillars, the features planned for each release phase, the game loop, the revenue model and a list of things the product will not build. Three fan profiles then show how different people might use it.
sections.why: Likely reason: the story gives the product its identity, and the pillars and phases turn that identity into a plan.
sections.watch_out: The game grades a fan's call against the model's estimate, so the grade is only as fair as that model. The text says the model must be published with its track record.

sections.name: File setup (part 10)
sections.title: Persona roster, naming and visual style
sections.what: Lists the five public persona names, one per sport, with the legend each is based on, the mentality they embody and the signature tool each uses. It explains why public names differ from internal codenames, and sets the visual direction, a reference table and the colour palette.
sections.why: Likely reason: public names avoid protected trademarks and athletes' personal rights, while the legend lineage keeps the story intact.
sections.watch_out: Internal codenames such as HITMAN and MAMBA appear in this document. The text says they must stay internal and out of public copy until counsel reviews the wording.

sections.name: File setup (part 11)
sections.title: Roadmap, risks and open decisions
sections.what: Lays out four delivery phases with exit criteria, a table of main risks with their mitigations, a list of facts not yet verified and a list of decisions the owner must make.
sections.why: Likely reason: a roadmap with exit criteria makes it clear when each phase is finished, and the risk list keeps known problems visible.
sections.watch_out: The numeric targets, such as 95 percent of numbers resolving to a source and about 200 test fans, are labelled suggested targets. Treat them as proposals, not agreed goals.

sections.name: File setup (part 12)
sections.title: Numbered source list
sections.what: A numbered list of sources grouped into capital and market, fans and India, big tech and leagues, regulation, startups, and data and research. Each in-text citation number points to one entry, so a reader can trace a claim to where it came from. The part visible here ends at entry 41, and later entries are outside this section.
sections.why: Likely reason: a numbered list lets each claim in the report be checked against its origin.
sections.watch_out: Some entries are news summaries, blogs or aggregator pages rather than original documents, so check key facts at the primary source.

sections.name: File setup (part 13)
sections.title: Source links for research claims
sections.what: Lists numbered sources from 42 to 85, each a link to an article, repository or record. The entries sit under headings such as AI harness engineering, trademarks and lineage, design references, open repositories and additional sources.
sections.why: Likely reason: to give the claims in the research a checkable source, and numbering lets other parts of the page point to a specific entry. Reason beyond that not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The trademark entries are research for naming, not legal clearance, and links can change or disappear over time.

sections.name: File setup (part 14)
sections.title: Footer and table of contents highlighting
sections.what: Shows the footer note on the research date, that recommendations are proposals, that athlete names are editorial references with no endorsement, and that the page is not legal advice. The script at the end collapses the table of contents on narrow screens and marks the section in view within that table of contents.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the long page usable on phones and shows the reader where they are. Reason for the disclaimer wording not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The research date is typed by hand and will not update, and the highlighting depends on the table of contents and section elements keeping their current names.

summary: A single web page that reviews the existing Hitman app, surveys how AI is changing sport, and sets out the planned ALTER EGO product, with numbered sources for its claims.
purpose: Gives the owner and the team one readable document covering the code review, the market research, the product plan, the design direction, the roadmap, the risks and the sources.
why: Likely reason: a single HTML page can be opened in any browser and shared as one link. The reason for this exact structure is not stated in the code.
how: The top of the file sets up the page, fonts and colour rules. A header and title block introduce the document. A contents list links to 17 numbered parts. Each part is a section with a heading, paragraphs, tables and callout boxes. Small numbered citations link to the sources list in part 17. The sections shown contain no scripts, so the page is static text and styling.
inputs: None at run time. The author wrote the text directly into the file. The page loads the Archivo font from Google Fonts when it opens. The header links to an external landing concept page on claude.ai.
outputs: A web page showing the report. The page does not save or send any data itself. Source and landing links open other websites.
risks: Many figures and claims come from outside news and reports. Part 16 says some facts are not yet verified. Legal points on gaming law, trademarks and personality rights are the authors' reading, and the document itself asks for counsel review. Outside sources may change or disappear, so a link may stop working.
debug: If the layout looks wrong, check the colour and layout rules near the top of the file. If the page looks unstyled, check that the Google Fonts link loads. If a citation number leads nowhere, check the matching entry in part 17. If a claim looks doubtful, open its numbered source before relying on it.
